The session begins.

The city is behind you now, only a smudge of smoke to the north. To the west the Sea of Swords has gone the colour of old pewter, and the sun is sliding toward it. Tamsin walks a half-step ahead with your pack hitched high on her shoulders, talking about who on the quay owes whom, and the cat pads along the verge, tail up, stopping now and then to smell the gorse.

Then the road bends around a stand of wind-bent pines, and there is a wagon.

It is a small two-wheeled carter's cart, tipped at an angle, one wheel sunk in the ditch. The mule is still in harness. It lifts its head, looks at you without much interest, and goes back to the grass. Sacks are lashed down under a canvas. Nobody is on the seat, nobody is in the ditch, nobody is on the road as far as you can see, and beyond the bend the road can't be seen at all. Something small and pale lies on the seat, too far away to make out.

Tamsin stops. The cat has stopped too, ears forward, staring at the trees.

"Well," Tamsin says, already shrugging the pack a little lower, "nobody leaves a mule standing. Not on this road." She looks back at you. The light is going. The Friendly Arm is still somewhere ahead.

Place: The Coast Way, south of Baldur's Gate
Time: Day 1 · afternoon

James's hand finds Tamsin's shoulder before the strap is off. She looks at him, then at the cat, and whatever she meant to say stays unsaid. The two of you step off the ruts into the pines. Needles muffle your boots, and the shadow under the branches is already cool. She crouches beside you with the pack against a trunk and fixes her eyes on the bend.

You close your hand around the warm coin and let go of your own eyes.

The world drops to a hand's height and turns grey-gold, sharp at the edges and blurred in the middle. Sound comes much louder. You hear the mule's teeth tearing grass, a gull far out over the water, and Tamsin breathing somewhere behind you. The smells hit hardest: gorse, mule, salt, crushed pine. Under all of it is something the cat dislikes before you do, sour and heavy, coming from the trees.

You send it east into the gorse, wide around the cart and low, then up the slope toward the alders that hide the bend.

The cat moves like a dropped shadow. It goes belly-low under the gorse and stops each time a twig ticks, and nothing in the trees turns its way.

Sixty or seventy feet in, among the alder roots, the sour smell has a shape. Somebody is crouched behind a fallen trunk, broad as a door, wrapped in a cloak the colour of dead bracken. Through the cat's eyes you see grey-green skin, a heavy jaw with a lower tusk showing, and a hand resting on a short spear, with three more stuck point-down in the leaf litter. The smell is rancid fat worked into old leather, which you have smelled before on night patrols. There's something else on top of it too: cold ash, from a fire that was put out and not cooked on. It's an orc, and it isn't watching the woods. It's watching the road, and more exactly it's watching the pines where you and Tamsin went in.

The cat's ears go flat. It doesn't go any closer.

You push it on along the slope, keeping the alders between it and the orc, toward the far side of the bend. Somewhere past the curve water runs over stone. Just as the road comes back into view the link starts to thin, like a rope paying out to its end. The cat is about a hundred feet from you now, and if it goes farther you lose its senses.

From there, at the very end of the link, you get one blurred look. About another hundred and fifty feet on, the road runs over a low stone bridge across a stream. A figure sits on the parapet, bigger than the one in the alders, with something long-hafted across its knees. Someone else stands in the road at the near end of the bridge. In the grey cat-light you can't make out more. The cat's whole body tells you something without words: *big one. iron. no.*

You bring it back.

It comes down the slope by a different line and slips under the mule's belly. The mule doesn't even shift. Then the cat jumps onto the tilted cart seat. Under the canvas the sacks smell of salt, plain sea salt, so much of it the cat sneezes. The pale thing on the seat is a flat plate of bone, wedged where a carter would sit. Someone has scratched into it with a knife point, in big clumsy capitals, Common letters cut deep enough to read even in this light:

**ODO FENNICK — SALT — 40 GOLD — WYRM ROCK - LT**

Out in the alders a low whistle sounds, two short notes, the way one man calls another. A moment later an answering note comes from the direction of the bridge.

Back where your own body crouches in the dark, blind and deaf, you feel Tamsin's fingers close hard on your forearm.

The grey-gold world snaps shut. Your own eyes come back slow and smeary, and the pines are darker than you left them. The air still smells of needles. Tamsin's hand is still tight on your arm.

"Nothing, for ages," she breathes. She talks fast even in a whisper. "Then a whistle, up there, left of the big dead alder. Two notes. Then one back from round the bend. Then a branch up there moved and didn't stop moving for a bit, like somebody shifting his weight. That's when I grabbed you. Sorry. Did I grab too hard?"

You work the crossbow by feel while she talks. You set the stirrup against your boot, draw the string back until it clicks into the nut, and seat the bolt in the groove. It makes almost no sound. The cat comes out of the gorse low and quick and presses itself against your shin. It doesn't sit.

Tamsin listens to all of it without interrupting, which isn't like her. At the name she blinks.

"Odo? Little Odo, ears like a pair of red mittens? He hauls salt down to the Arm every tenday. He owes Grell on the fish steps two silver and has done since Midsummer." She looks over at the tilted cart, the mule, the canvas. "Forty gold. You could buy that whole cart and the mule and Odo's hat for less than forty gold. Who do they think pays that?"

When you tell her to get behind the cart and stay down, she looks at you for a moment. Then she nods once and says "Behind the cart," flat, like a dock clerk reading back a delivery. She pulls the pack straps tight across her chest so it won't swing.

Then the road answers for everyone.

Somebody comes round the bend at a walk, not hurrying, boots loud on the ruts. It's an orc, not the big one. He's broad and bare-armed in stiff hide, with a greataxe resting on one shoulder the way a labourer carries a shovel and two javelins in a sling across his back. He stops on the far side of the cart, about fifty feet from your pines, and puts himself where you can see him clearly. The mule glances at him and goes back to eating.

He doesn't look at the alders. He looks straight into the shadow where you're crouched, and he can see you there.

"You in trees," he calls. His Common is thick but slow and careful, like a lesson he's said before. "Road costs. Five gold each head. Cart stays. You come to bridge, you pay chief, you walk on to fat inn. Nobody hurt." He moves the axe on his shoulder a little. "You run north, also fine. Nobody chase." He waits, then adds, as if he'd been told to say it, "Chief says: no shooting. Shooting makes it cost more."

Up in the alders a branch creaks. The lookout is moving, keeping the pines in view.

The orc watches you come out of the shadow the way a dock hand watches a crate being swung over his head: no alarm, just attention. His eyes go to the crossbow pointed at the dirt, then to your free hand, then back to your face. The axe stays on his shoulder.

He listens all the way through. When you say *forty gold* he nods slowly, as if you've finally got to the right part of the lesson.

"Little man alive," he says. "Eats much. Cries some, at night." He thinks about the rest of your question and shakes his head once. "Not on bridge. In wood. Safe. Dry." He says the last two words carefully, like they were given to him to say.

He tips his chin at the cart, at the pale plate on the seat.

"Note is for carrying. Somebody finds cart, somebody carries note north. Fist pays. Fist always pays." He doesn't say it like a boast. He says it like a man telling you the ferry runs on the hour. "You carry note, chief likes you more."

Then he looks past you into the pines, where Tamsin is. He can't have heard her move, but he looks right at the spot anyway.

"You see little man, chief decides. Not me." He shifts the axe from one shoulder to the other, and you can hear the hide creak. "You and porter, come. Bow stays down. You walk in front, I walk behind, so." He holds up both broad hands with the fingers spread, then does it again: *twenty*. Twenty paces, maybe. "Lookout walks with us, up in trees. He does not shoot unless you shoot."

Up the slope the alder branch creaks again. It's closer to the road now.

Behind you, low enough that only you can hear, Tamsin lets out a breath. "Cries at night," she murmurs. "That's Odo all right." She doesn't come out yet. She's waiting for you.

The orc waits too. He's planted at the edge of the road with the bend and the bridge behind him and the cart's tilted wheel at his knee, and the bone plate is still sitting on the seat a few feet from his hand. The sun has dropped another finger's width toward the sea.

"Fair enough" is answer enough for the orc. He watches you sling the crossbow across your back, and his eyes stay on the stock until it's settled against your shoulder blade. Then they follow you to the cart.

You go slowly. The mule lets you near without lifting its head, and its neck is warm and dusty under your palm. The bone plate is wedged tight into the seat and you have to work it loose. The cut letters feel rough under your thumb. As you slide it inside your cloak, the canvas beside you flaps back a hand's width. On the corner of the nearest salt sack is a stamp in black ink: a pair of spread wings, square-edged, the kind a merchant burns into a die.

The orc doesn't move. When the plate goes into your cloak he gives one slow nod, as if a crate has landed where it was meant to.

"Tamsin. Come on out, stay at my left side. Pip, up."

Needles crunch, and Tamsin comes out of the pines with the pack tight across her chest. She falls in on your left, close enough that her elbow nearly brushes yours. The cat comes faster than she does. It runs up your leg and back the moment you crouch and settles across your shoulders, low and heavy, claws working through the cloak to the leather underneath. You can feel its heart going quick against your neck.

When you ask his name, the orc looks at you for a moment. Nobody on this road has asked him that before.

"Hurgash," he says. He tries your name, carefully, the way he says everything. "James." Then he steps back off the ruts and waits for you to pass him. He lets you get well ahead, counts it out under his breath, and falls in behind. The axe stays on his shoulder.

You walk.

The road curves left around the alders. A little after you start, the trees above you start to talk. Something moves along the slope at your pace, a branch giving and springing back, a scuff of leaves, then quiet, then the same again a few yards on. The lookout isn't trying to hide it. He wants you to hear him.

"Five gold a head," Tamsin says under her breath, staring straight ahead. "Ten for us. That's what Grell clears in a month on the fish steps, and the Duke's supposed to keep this road for nothing." She glances up at your shoulder. "Cat's shaking."

It is.

The bend opens out. The ground drops gently to the stream, which runs fast and shallow over flat brown stones. The bridge crosses it in one low arch, built of old grey stone with a waist-high parapet and moss in the joints. On the far bank a second orc leans on a spear among the reeds. You didn't see him through the cat's eyes. He doesn't straighten up.

The big one is still sitting on the parapet, right where the cat saw him.

Up close he's broader than Hurgash and a head taller. Under a cloak of patched wool he wears a chain shirt, dull and well oiled. The greataxe lies across his knees with both his hands resting on the haft. He wears his hair in thick braids with iron rings worked into them, and there's grey at the temples. He watches the three of you come down the last stretch of road, and nothing on his face changes.

At about thirty feet off, one of his hands leaves the axe. It goes to his chest, where something hangs on a leather thong over the chain. He closes his fingers around it, frowns, and lets it fall. In the low sun it turns once and catches the light. It's a heavy silver coin, and the face turned toward you shows a woman's profile, smiling. You know that face. A worn copy of it hangs at your own throat.

He doesn't look at it again. He looks at you.

"I am Ushkar," he says. His Common is better than Hurgash's, deep and in no hurry, the voice of a man used to having his first word be the last. "Hurgash says you do not shoot. Good." His eyes go to Tamsin, then to the cat on your shoulders, then to the front of your cloak where the bone plate sits. "Ten gold for two heads. The cart and the salt stay with me. And you have my note."

 (Out of game: none of these four needed a roll. The story already plays each one: you take the plate, pat the mule, Tamsin comes out to your left, and Pip climbs to your shoulder. Nothing about them was uncertain.)

James stops at the foot of the bridge, well out of reach of the axe. He counts the coins out one at a time, and the gold catches what is left of the sun as each piece goes down. Ten small discs make a short stack on the mossy parapet between them.

Ushkar watches every coin. When the stack is done he reaches over and slides it toward himself with two fingers. He doesn't count it again. It goes into a pouch at his belt, and that's the end of it.

Beside James, Tamsin lets out a breath through her nose. It's the sound of somebody adding up ten gold against a month on the fish steps and not liking the total. She says nothing.

Then James draws his own coin out over his cloak.

Ushkar's eyes go to it at once and stay there. For a moment the two coins hang in the same low light, a few yards apart: his heavy and sharp-edged, James's worn almost to nothing. The same smiling woman is on both. James feels his own coin against his knuckles. It is warm, as it always is, maybe a little warmer.

Ushkar's hand goes up to his chest and closes on the thong.

"Neither," he says. "Paid. A woman came over this bridge in spring, walking south, alone. No gold. She gave me this and said it was worth more." His mouth moves, not quite a smile. "It was not." He turns the coin over in his thick fingers and holds it out on its thong so the other face catches the light.

There is no second face of the Lady on the back. That side has been scraped flat and cut again by an unskilled hand pressing hard with a knife point. The scratches show an eye, wide open, with no lid drawn and a deep gouge for a pupil.

"It came like this," Ushkar says. He lets it fall back against the chain. "It is warm. Since you came down the road." He doesn't say whether he likes that.

When James taps the cloak over the bone plate, the chief's attention comes back to business, and it comes back quickly.

"You want to see him." Ushkar thinks about it with his hands on the haft. "Not the camp." He raises his voice without seeming to try. "Hurgash. The little man. Bring him to the trees."

Behind you, boots leave the road. Hurgash goes up the slope into the alders without a word, and the branches close behind him. From the sound of it he isn't going far, but he isn't going near either. Up on the slope the lookout's branch creaks once and goes still.

"You wait," Ushkar says. "He comes. You look at him. He goes back." The sun is down to a red rim above the sea, and the stream has gone dark under the arch. Then his eyes settle on James, flat and patient, the way a man looks at a hand he hasn't seen played yet.

"Save the Fist the trip," he repeats. "Forty gold. From your hand?"

He waits for your answer.

 (Out of game: I didn't roll any of these four. Paying, showing the coin and asking are things James simply does, and they had no uncertain outcome. His request to see Odo was true and in Ushkar's own interest, since he wants the note carried, so he agreed without a check.)

James leaves the coin hanging over his cloak. It's warm against his knuckles when he lets go of it, warmer than the evening.

Ushkar's eyes go to it again while James names his terms, then back to James's face. *From my hand* makes his jaw shift slightly, as if he's testing a tooth. *Mule, salt and all* gets nothing from him at all.

When James is done, Ushkar leaves a long silence. The stream runs loud under the arch. In the reeds on the far bank the spear orc has straightened up after all, and he's watching.

"Odo, forty," Ushkar says. "Cart and mule, ten more." He lifts one hand off the axe haft and lets it fall. "Salt I keep. Winter is long in the hills. Meat needs salt."

He gives that a moment to settle, then gives the rest.

"You pay me, not the Fist. Then the bone comes back to my hand. At the fat inn you say the road cost ten. Nothing more." His eyes go to the front of James's cloak, where the tally sits, and stay there. "That is the price."

Beside James, Tamsin breathes in to say something. She looks at the cloak, then at the orc, and closes her mouth again.

Then James asks about the woman, and Ushkar's hand goes to the thong on his chest. He doesn't seem to notice he's done it. His thumb runs over the cut face of the coin and stops in the gouge of the pupil.

"Human," he says. "Older than you. Hair short, grey like iron. Good boots, much walked. A staff with no iron on it." He thinks. "She walked fast, like somebody late. Up to the bridge she looked back up the road twice. The way people look when someone walks behind them."

"Her words." He frowns, getting them right. "'I have no gold. Take this. It is worth more. Don't spend it.' Then she looked at the eye, and at me, and said: 'Let it watch the road.'" He lets the coin fall back against the chain. "She asked me one thing. Who I take the toll for. I told her: me." The not-quite-smile comes back and goes. "Then she went south, over the bridge. To the fat inn, I think. She did not stop."

When James says the coin rarely pays the way you expect but does pay, Ushkar looks at him longer than he has at anything else on this bridge. He doesn't answer.

Up on the slope, the alders start cracking. It's heavy, careless feet coming down, branches whipping back, and under it a thin, injured voice, close to tears: "—*told* you, the rope's on the *same* wrist, you've done the *same wrist* twice—"

Tamsin's head comes round. "That's him," she whispers. "That's Odo."

Ushkar doesn't look toward the trees. He's waiting for James's answer to his price.

James lets his eyes go up the slope while the alders crack and the thin voice gets closer. Ushkar sees where he's looking and waits too.

When James names the price, the chief doesn't move. *Fifty* gets a slow nod. *The bone goes back to your hand* gets another. When James raises one finger and talks about Odo's mouth, Ushkar's eyes narrow a little. He isn't angry. He's working out what it will cost him.

"He talks," Ushkar says. "I know. Hurgash fed him two days. Everyone in the wood knows how he talks." He's quiet for a moment while the stream runs under the arch. "You tell me straight. Good. A man who promises me the little man's mouth is lying to me." His hands settle on the axe haft again. "Fifty. The bone to my hand. Ten at the fat inn. The rest is his."

When James mentions the coin, the chief doesn't look down at it. He looks at the worn one hanging over James's cloak.

"I do not spend it," he says. He doesn't say anything else about it.

Across Ushkar's shoulders the cat goes stiff. Its claws close through the cloak, and its ears turn, not toward the trees, but down and to the right, toward the dark under the bridge arch where the water runs. It holds still like that for a breath, then flattens again against James's neck.

Tamsin hears the murmur and answers just as low. "Cart's back round the bend, James. I'll keep you between me and the spear instead." She slips around his back to his right side, on the uphill side, away from the reeds, and goes up the verge as Hurgash comes out of the alders.

Odo Fennick arrives a step ahead of the orc on a short rope. He's small and round-shouldered, in a carter's smock gone grey with two days of wood dirt. Even in this light his ears are a remarkable red. His wrists are tied in front of him, and the rope's end is wrapped around Hurgash's fist. A fresh bramble scratch runs across one cheek. He walks on his own, and when Hurgash stops at the edge of the road he stops too, blinking at the bridge, at the chief, and at the stranger with a cat on his shoulders.

Then he sees Tamsin.

"Tamsin? Quay Tamsin? What are you doing out—" His voice cracks. "Is that my mule I heard? Is the mule all right? They left her in the *ditch*—"

"Mule's eating, Odo. Stand still." Tamsin turns his wrists over in her hands, gently, the way you'd check a crate for a split board. She looks at his face and the scratch, then at his feet, and steps back to where James can see her. "Rope's burned him raw on the left. They did tie the same wrist twice, the fools. Bramble on his face. Nothing broken. He's been fed." She sniffs. "Better than he eats at home, by the smell."

"It was *mutton*," Odo says, injured, as if someone had accused him.

Hurgash stands at the edge of the ruts holding the rope. He looks to his chief and does nothing else.

Ushkar hasn't looked at Odo once. He's looking at James's hand, where it rests near the purse.

"He stands," the chief says. "Nothing broken. Now the gold."

He waits. The sun is a thin red line on the sea behind him, and the light on the bridge is going grey.

James unties the purse and counts the coins out onto the moss, one at a time, the way he did before. The last of the light is grey now and the gold hardly shines, but Ushkar watches every piece land. When the stack reaches fifty, James takes the bone plate from inside his cloak and lays it on top with the cut letters facing the chief.

"Fifty. And your bone. The road cost ten."

Ushkar reaches out and takes the tally first. He turns it once in his fingers, reads it or just looks at it, and pushes it into his belt behind the pouch. Then he sweeps the gold off the parapet into his palm in two handfuls and drops it into the pouch. The pouch hangs heavier now. He doesn't count it.

"Hurgash, cut him loose, if you'd be so kind. I'll walk him back to his mule myself."

Hurgash looks at his chief. Ushkar gives a short nod. The messenger takes a knife from his belt and saws through the rope between Odo's wrists. It's quick and careful, and he keeps the blade well away from the raw skin. The rope drops into the ruts. Odo stands there holding his own hands in front of him, as if he isn't sure they're his to move yet.

I put a hand on Tamsin's shoulder before she can drop the pack, and keep my voice low.

"Not yet. The cat's looking at the trees, not the cart. Mules stand still for bandits too." I ease us both off the road into the shadow of the pines, crossbow unslung but not loaded yet.

"Keep your eyes on that treeline and the bend. If anything moves, squeeze my arm. I'm going to be blind for a bit."

Then I crouch, rest my hand on the coin at my throat, and slip into the cat's senses. I send it low through the gorse toward the trees it was staring at, circling wide so it comes up behind whatever is there. I want to know what it smelled, and whether anyone is waiting past the bend. On the way back it can hop up on the cart seat and tell me what that pale thing is.

I let go of the cat and come back into my own eyes fast, blinking against the dark under the pines.

"What did you see?" I breathe to Tamsin, not taking my eyes off the alders. While she answers, I load a bolt into the crossbow by feel, slow and quiet.

"Listen. There's an orc behind a fallen trunk up in the alders, maybe seventy feet, with spears. Two more at a stone bridge past the bend, one of them big. They've been watching this spot, and they just whistled to each other. The note on the cart is a ransom: the carter, Odo Fennick, forty gold. So they want money more than blood, for now."

I glance at her. "If this goes bad, you get behind the cart and stay down. Don't be brave."

I lower the crossbow so the bolt points at the dirt. I don't unload it. Then I step one pace out of the pines, just far enough that he can see my hands, and leave Tamsin and the cat in the shadow behind me.

"No shooting," I call back, easy and even, the way you'd talk to a sergeant at a checkpoint. "Fair road, fair toll. I can respect that."

I nod at the tilted cart. "But your chief left a note on the seat. Odo Fennick, forty gold. Tell me straight, friend: is the little man alive? Is he at the bridge with your chief?"

I let that sit a moment, then shrug.

"Because if he is, I'm walking to the fat inn anyway, and I'm the sort of fellow who carries messages. Maybe I carry gold too. But I don't pay for a dead man, and I don't pay for one I haven't seen." I spread my free hand. "So let's go see your chief. Me and my porter. We'll talk tolls on the bridge like civilised folk."

"Fair enough." I sling the crossbow across my back, still loaded but out of my hands. Then I walk to the cart, slow so he can watch every step, and take the bone plate off the seat. I tuck it inside my cloak.

"If I'm carrying the note, I'll hold on to it." I give the mule's neck a pat as I pass. Then, over my shoulder, without raising my voice: "Tamsin. Come on out, stay at my left side. Pip, up."

I crouch so the cat can climb to my shoulder, then straighten up and look at the orc.

"Lead on. Well, follow on." I nod toward the bend. "I'm James. What do they call you? If I'm going to have an axe at my back for twenty paces, I'd like to know whose it is."

Then I start walking toward the bridge at an easy pace, hands loose and in plain sight. I keep half an ear on the alders above us.

I stop at the foot of the bridge, a respectful distance from the axe, and count ten gold out of my purse slowly, so he can watch every coin. Then I set them in a little stack on the parapet between us.

"Ten for two heads. Fair road, fair toll."

I don't step back yet. I hook a finger under the cord at my throat and draw my own coin out over the cloak, letting it hang there in the same low sun. The same smiling woman looks out from it, only mine is worn nearly smooth.

"You and I keep the same company, it seems," I say quietly. "She doesn't usually hand those out to men who sit on bridges and wait. So either you won it, or she sent you something. I'd like to know which."

I let that sit a moment, then tap my cloak where the bone plate is.

"Now, the note. Hurgash says the little man is alive and dry. I believe him; he strikes me as a man who repeats what he's told, honestly. But I'll be carrying forty gold's worth of words to the Fist, and they'll ask me if I saw Odo with my own eyes. I'd rather say yes. Take me to him, or bring him here, and I'll carry your note to the inn tonight. Maybe I can save the Fist the trip altogether."

I keep my coin out over the cloak and don't put it away. If his is warming, I want it to keep warming.

"From my hand," I say. "Once I've seen him standing on his own two feet with nothing broken. Forty for Odo. And the cart goes with him: mule, salt and all. A carter with no cart is just a man who cries at night, and that's no use to anybody."

I let him chew on that for a moment, then nod at the thong on his chest.

"And while we wait, tell me about the woman. What did she look like, which way did she go after the bridge, and what exactly did she say when she gave you that? Her words, not yours." I give him a small, crooked smile. "You think it wasn't worth more. I've had that coin's sister at my throat long enough to tell you she rarely pays the way you expect. But she does pay."

Tamsin stays at my left. Out of the corner of my eye I keep watch on the alders, waiting for Hurgash to come back with Odo.

I don't answer right away. I let my eyes go up the slope toward Odo's complaining, so Ushkar sees I'm waiting on that before anything else. Then I look back at him.

"Fifty, then. Forty for Odo, ten for the cart and the mule. You keep the salt. Winter's long, I won't argue with that." I tap my cloak over the tally. "And the bone goes back to your hand the moment the gold does. I've no use for it."

I hold up one finger.

"The inn's another matter, so I'll be straight with you. I'll say the road cost ten, and I'll say nothing more. But I can't sew that little man's mouth shut. He'll tell it his own way, crying, to anyone who buys him a drink. So if the Fist comes down this road, it won't be on my word." I give a small shrug. "Better you hear that from me now than find out later I lied to you."

I nod at the coin on his chest.

"And she told you not to spend it. I'd listen. Whoever she was, she was looking back up the road for a reason."

Then I glance at Tamsin without turning my head. "Go and look at him when he's down. See if he's hurt anywhere," I murmur, "and keep the cart between you and the spear." My hand rests near my purse but doesn't open it. Nothing moves until Odo is standing in the road.

I open the purse and count out fifty gold onto the parapet, slow and even like before. Then I take the bone plate out of my cloak and lay it on top of the stack, the cut letters facing him.

"Fifty. And your bone. The road cost ten." I nod toward Odo. "Hurgash, cut him loose, if you'd be so kind. I'll walk him back to his mule myself."

I tuck my coin back under the cloak, but I keep my hand on it. Without moving my head I let my eyes drift down to the dark under the arch where Pip was staring, then back to Ushkar.

"One more thing, chief, since we're being straight with each other," I say quietly. "My cat doesn't like whatever's under your bridge. If that's one of yours, fine. If it isn't, you might want to know."

I give Ushkar a short nod, the way you'd nod to an officer whose orders you've decided to follow, and turn my back on the axe without hurrying.

"Come on, Odo. Let's get your girl out of the ditch."

Back at the bend I put my shoulder to the sunk wheel while Tamsin takes the mule's head and Odo fusses at the harness. "On three. Tamsin, lead her forward slow. Odo, push where I push, not where you think."

While we strain at it I keep my voice low, for the two of them only.

"Once she's out, we turn her south and cross that bridge at a walk. We've paid. We don't stop, we don't talk to anyone in the reeds, and nobody looks under the arch." I glance at Odo. "And when we get to the inn, little man, you can cry to whoever you like. But first you tell me everything about those two days. Who came to the camp, who they talked about, and whether anyone else in that wood had a coin like the chief's."

I fall into step on Tamsin's side of the mule, so she's between me and the gorse and Odo is on the other flank.

"Go on," I say quietly. "Say it before it chokes you. Sixty gold to a man on a bridge. I know."

While she gets it out I reach across the mule's neck and take Odo's left hand, the rope-burned wrist, palm up. I cup my other hand over it, and a little warm gold light leaks out between my fingers, the Lady's light, just one die's worth. "Hold still. That'll stop it weeping by the time we reach the inn."

Then, to both of them:

"Odo, two things. Those sacks had a stamp on them, black wings, square-edged. Whose mark is that? And that bright silver: where did the sack come from? Did someone bring it to the chief, or was it there when they took you?" I glance back once at the grey hump of the bridge. "A man who doesn't ask where you live doesn't need your family to pay. He already knows who's paying."

I let the cart roll on a few paces before I answer, and I keep my voice down.

"You're right to be angry, and you did well to keep your mouth shut. That's harder than shooting." I tap my temple. "But the bone isn't lost. I read it twice. *Odo Fennick, salt, forty gold, Wyrm Rock, L-T.* LT isn't a name a carter's family knows. It's a rank. Lieutenant. Somebody at Wyrm's Rock was meant to get that note and pay out of a grey linen sack of new silver. Ushkar keeping the bone doesn't change that. It just means he believes I'm a man who keeps his word, and I'd like him to go on believing it a while."

I glance back toward the dark where the bridge was.

"And I will say the road cost ten. The road did cost ten. Odo cost fifty, and that's Odo's tale to tell." I look over the mule's neck at him. "Which brings me to you, little man. When we walk into the Arm, you're going to want to tell the whole common room that the Fist pays orcs. Don't. Not tonight, not to the room. Somebody in that room drinks with a lieutenant. Cry about the mule, cry about the salt, curse Blackwing for selling you salt orcs like. But the silver and the Fist you keep for me, and for whoever I say. Can you do that?"

Then, to Tamsin, quieter:

"Two more things to watch for at the inn. Anyone in a Fist tabard who seems a little too glad to see Odo, or a little too sorry. And a grey-haired woman with good boots and a staff with no iron on it. She came this way in spring, and she was looking over her shoulder. If anyone at the Arm remembers her, I want to know."

I scratch the cat behind the ear and lengthen my stride toward the rise, watching for lights.

"You'll know because I'll be standing next to them," I tell Odo. "Nobody else. Not even if they say my name."

I slow us down at the crest, letting the mule tug, while I look at the two figures by the gate. Before we come into the lantern light I want to know if they're Fist tabards or the inn's own men.

"Tamsin, take the halter. I'll walk at the back with the cart." I lift the cat off my shoulders and set it on the empty cart bed. "Pip, stay up here and look sorry for yourself."

Then we go down the slope at an honest walk. Odo is in front with his raw wrist and his long face, and the empty cart rattles. That's exactly what we are: three tired people and a mule who lost a season's salt on the road.

At the gate I nod to whoever's leaning there, easy and friendly.

"Evening. Room for three and a mule? Our friend here had a bad two days on the Coast Way."

I fish five silver out of my purse and press it into Fen's hand. "For the mule. Give her the good hay, she earned it." I nod to Dorra. "Sheathed. You have my word."

Then I scoop Pip off the cart bed and set him back on my shoulders.

On the way across the yard I lean down to Odo and speak low and quick.

"Change of plan. You walk in first, straight to the corner table, and you get Wenna up out of that chair before she puts another coin down. Hug her, cry, whatever you like, but her purse closes and she stands up. You're the ransom she was paying for, so she doesn't owe anyone at that table a copper more. If anyone says the hand isn't finished, look at me."

To Tamsin: "Find the cook. Boots and a staff with no iron, spring. Then come back to me."

I walk in behind Odo and stop just inside the door, out of the press. I don't go near the table. I just watch who's dealing, who's sitting closest to Wenna's purse, and how they take it when the carter they were supposed to be ransoming walks in on his own two feet. My hand is over the warm coin, and it stays there.

I cross the room unhurried, Pip heavy on my shoulders, and stop at the corner table. I keep my hands on my belt, well away from the cards, and I don't sit.

"I speak for her," I say pleasantly, loud enough for Wenna and no further. "And the hand's dead, Master Ivo. Her cards are lying face-up for the whole room, so there's nothing left to play. She takes back her nine, you keep your five, and everyone has a drink to Odo."

Then I lean in a little, still smiling, and drop my voice so it's just for him.

"Three fingers on the long edge, forefinger on the end, and you square it toward yourself. You deal a lovely second. Soft. In Tethyr we broke thumbs for less, but this is a nice inn and Dorra hates mopping." I tap the table once beside his deck, not on it. "So: her nine back. And one question while you count it. Who told you to help her make it up to *fifty*?"

I don't look at the deck. I keep my hands on my belt until the heat at my throat fades back to warm. Then I reach out one finger and slide the cards back across the table to him, slowly, until they're sitting square in front of his flat hands.

"I don't sit any more, Master Ivo," I say quietly. "I made a promise to a lady with better luck than either of us. Keep your five. And I've already forgotten your deal, so long as nobody else in this room learns it the hard way tonight."

I straighten up and give him a pleasant nod, the way you'd nod to an officer from someone else's regiment.

"Your satchel strap's wound the way dispatch riders wind it. That's a Tethyrian habit too. Maybe we'll trade war stories another night."

Then I turn my back on the table and step over beside Odo and Wenna, with Pip heavy on my shoulders, so I'm standing next to the carter when the corporal in the red tabard reaches us. I put on a tired, friendly face and wait for her to speak first.

I keep the tired, friendly face and don't hurry the answer, the way you don't hurry a sergeant with a tablet.

"The road cost ten, Corporal. Five a head, me and my porter, paid to a big fellow on the bridge with an axe across his knees. Then we walked on." That's the truth, and it's my promise. I nod at Odo, who is clutching his sister and the purse. "His two days are his own story. He'll tell it better with mutton in him than I could standing here. Let him sit down and eat first. He's earned that much."

Then, as if it's only idle curiosity between two people who've both worn a uniform:

"That line of yours that goes up to the Rock with the morning post. Who reads road business up there? A lieutenant?"

While I say it I watch her face, not her stylus: whether she writes *ten*, whether her eyes go to Odo again, and what she does with the word *lieutenant*.

I meet her look and let a small, rueful smile show, like a man caught out by someone sharper than he expected.

"Nobody told me, Corporal. I guessed, and you've just told me I guessed right." I keep my voice down to match hers. "Old habit. In Tethyr, when coin went out of a regiment's chest to buy back men from the wrong side of a river, a captain never put his name to it. It was always a lieutenant. Someone senior enough to open the chest and junior enough to blame."

I glance once at Odo on his bench by the hearth and then back at her.

"I gave a man my word on that bridge, and the word was ten. I keep my word, even to men on bridges. But you've been sitting at the end of this bar since the thaw, counting who comes back and when, and it doesn't sit right with you. I can see that much." I tip my head toward the stair, away from the corner table. "When Odo's eaten, come and find me. Somewhere quieter than this room, and I'll buy the drink. I think we might want the same thing."

I give her a short nod, the kind one uniform gives another. Then I step past her toward the kitchen arch, where Tamsin is waiting with flour on her sleeve.

I look down at the coin for a moment before I answer. Lying to Tamsin feels like a poor way to repay three loaves.

"I don't know yet," I say quietly. "The Lady doesn't give me a list of her people. But she gave a man on a bridge a coin and told him to let it watch the road. And this whole evening the coin at my throat has been warmer than a coin ought to be. So, maybe. Or maybe she's somebody the Lady wanted me to find." I touch her floury sleeve. "Either way, you did better in that kitchen than I did out there. Thank you."

Then I tilt my head a fraction toward the corner table without looking at it.

"Don't turn round. Master Ivo, grey coat, the patience game nobody's playing. He's writing something small and neat on a scrap of paper. I want to know where that paper goes: into his coat, into the satchel, or into somebody else's hand. Above all, whether he gives it to anyone who's riding north tonight. You're a porter with bread, and nobody looks at porters. Stay by the arch and eat slowly."

I scratch Pip under the chin.

"I'm going out to the well. The corporal wants a word once she's finished with the Fennicks. If Ivo gets up to leave, come and find me. Don't follow him. Just tell me."

Then I go back through the common room at an easy pace and out into the yard. I find a spot by the well where I can see both the keep door and the gate, put my back to the stones, and wait for Strake.

I look at the hand she's laid flat on the back of the tablet, then up at her face.

"Off the wax is kind of you, Corporal. But my word on that bridge wasn't to the wax. It was to a man with an axe. I said the road cost ten and I'd say nothing more. If I break it to you out here by the well, you'd be a fool to trust anything else I tell you, and you don't strike me as a fool."

I nudge her cup an inch further from Pip's nose.

"But I told him the truth too: I can't sew Odo's mouth shut. That little man has kept quiet all evening because I asked him to, and he'll talk to whoever I stand next to." I tip my head at the lit doorway. "So here's my offer. Finish your drink. Then I'll bring Odo out here, stand beside you, and he can tell you his two days himself: who paid, how much, and what he saw by the orcs' fire. You'll hear things in it you'll want to hear somewhere nobody's listening."

I let that settle, then ask the question I actually came out here with, quietly.

"Before I fetch him, tell me one thing in return. When *returned* goes up to the Rock in that bag, and the man who reads it sees his book shows he didn't pay, is that a man you'd want reading what Odo has to say? Or do you need it to go to someone else?"

"Seven and seven," I say quietly. "That's a number worth carrying to the right door. We'll find the door."

I scratch Pip once between the ears and leave him sitting on the well rim. "Stay, Pip. Watch the bag." I glance at the mailbag on its hook. If anyone but the driver goes near it, I want to know.

Then I go back inside at the same easy pace. On the way past the kitchen arch I catch Tamsin's eye and lift my eyebrows: *anything?*

At the hearth bench I crouch down beside Odo, so I'm just a friendly face at mutton level, and give Wenna my warmest smile.

"Mistress Fennick, I need to borrow your brother for five minutes. The mule's fretting in the stable and won't settle for the lad, and I think she wants Odo." I put a hand on his shoulder. "Bring your bread, Odo. Wenna, keep his seat warm and his cup full. He'll be right back."

Then, low, as he gets up: "Remember who you talk to. The one I'm standing next to. Out by the well."

I look at the folded paper against her chest for a long moment, and I don't reach for it.

"Honest answer? I don't know yet. I've been in this country three days." I keep my voice as low as hers. "But I know whose door it isn't. Not your captain's, not anyone's at the Rock, and not in that bag." I tip my head at the mailbag on its hook. "Keep that list where it's been since the thaw. Next to your skin. Don't copy it, don't send it."

I glance at the lit doorway.

"One more thing you should know before morning. The man in the grey coat at the corner table, Ivo. He was dealing seconds to Wenna to push her purse up to fifty. Then, once Odo walked in on his own feet, he wrote a little note in a neat hand and put it in his coat. If that note goes north tonight, Hale knows by tomorrow that his carter came back without the Rock paying, and who walked him in. I'd like to know which way Ivo rides, and whether he goes near that driver."

I touch the coin under my collar.

"As for the door: I owe a lady in the Lady's Hall more than I can count, and I'm her errand-runner now. Tymora's priests have money, the ear of patriars, and no love for anyone who fixes the odds. That's one door. There may be a better one. A grey-haired woman went south from here in spring, asking if anyone was hunting her. I think she was carrying the same kind of number you are." I meet her look. "So tell me, Corporal. Is there anyone in the Fist above Hale you'd trust with your own name on this? Not your captain. Someone he'd be afraid of."

"Then that's the door," I say quietly. "And the silver's under a bedroll in the Cloakwood, beside a man who doesn't spend what he's given. Ushkar put every coin back, Corporal. A man who does that is either afraid of whose money it is, or he's keeping it to show someone. Either way I know where it sleeps."

I pick Pip up off the well rim and settle him on my shoulders.

"You've carried that list since the thaw. Carry it a few days more. Don't change anything. Your report goes in at first light, same as always, with *returned* beside Odo's name." I nod toward the bag. "I'd count it a favour if you were standing by that cart when the bell rings, the way you always are. If a grey coat comes out to hand the driver something, I'd like to know whose name is on the front."

Then I give her the same short nod as before and go back inside.

At the counter by the stair I find Brannoc and his ledger, and lean on the wood like a tired man who's finally thinking about bed.

"A room for me and my porter. Something with a door that locks, two pallets, and a fire if you've got one." I put a gold piece down. "And while I'm here: I may have a letter for the north bag tomorrow. Has the bag much in it tonight? I'd hate mine to sit under a stack." I glance idly at the ledger, as if I don't care at all, and watch whether his eyes go to the corner table.

"That's all, master. Thank you." I tip my head at the drover with the jug. "Go save your tap."

I pocket the key and go back to the kitchen arch. On the way I don't look at the corner.

"Room six, top of the stair, window on the yard," I murmur to Tamsin. "His note isn't in the north box. Four letters, none of them his. So either he hands it over at the bell, or he gives it to someone tonight. Finish your crust and come up."

Upstairs I bolt the door, give the sticky shutter a shove from the bottom and crack it a hand's width, so I can see the post cart and the well without showing a light. I build up the fire low and set the lantern behind the bed where it won't throw my shadow on the shutter.

Then I set Pip on the sill.

"Watch the yard, Pip. Anyone who goes near that cart or that bag, or anyone in a grey coat who comes out after the house goes quiet, you wake me. Paw on my face, I don't care." I scratch his ears. "Tamsin, we take turns. You sleep first. I'll wake you past midnight, and I want to be at this window myself well before half past six."

I pull a chair to the shutter, put the loaded crossbow across my knees, and sit with my back to the wall, watching the dark yard.

I'm up before the horse finishes sidling. The crossbow goes against the wall, still loaded, and I touch Tamsin's shoulder on the way past.

"Anything's happening," I whisper. "The caravan guard's riding north with something in his jerkin. Bolt the door behind me and watch from the shutter. Pip stays with you."

Then I'm down the stair fast and quiet. The elven boots make no sound on the worn steps. I go through the common room without hurrying where people can see me, and out into the yard. I don't run across the mud. I walk straight to the gate at a soldier's quick pace, hands empty and in plain sight, and call out before he can get his leg over.

"Hold a moment, friend. Dorra's right, that road's no place for one man at night. I came up it this afternoon." I stop at the horse's shoulder, beside Dorra, and keep my voice low and easy. "I saw you lose your shirt at that table. Then the man who dealt it bought you a jug. So whatever he's paying you to carry north tonight, I'm guessing it doesn't cover your debts. Tell me what it is and who it's for, and maybe we can find you a better bargain than riding past an orc bridge in the dark."

"The better bargain is the one where you're alive tomorrow, Pell." I keep my voice low and nod at Dorra. "She's right. The watch on that bridge shoots first. You shook his hand to carry a letter into Hale's hand. You didn't promise to die doing it."

I take five gold from my purse and hold it where he can see it, but I don't give it to him yet.

"So here's what I'm offering. You don't break your word. The letter still goes to Hale, in his own hand, from *the Arm*, exactly as you were told. But you ride at first light with the post cart instead of alone at midnight. That's safer company, and the bridge is in daylight. And before then you let me look at it. Upstairs, ten minutes, with you standing there the whole time. I'm no clerk, but I can lift plain black wax and set it back so the man who sealed it couldn't tell." I flex my fingers, and a faint warmth shimmers over them, a little trick of the Lady's. "Nobody will ever know it was opened, Ivo included. You lose nothing, and you're five gold to the good."

I glance at the keep door, then back at him.

"And if anyone asks why you left late, the truth is enough: Dorra wouldn't let go of your bridle."

**What worked**

- **The world ran on its own.** Ushkar, Strake, Ivo and Pell all had their own reasons and their own limits. None of them felt like a quest-giver waiting for me. Ushkar answering "tell me straight" with respect instead of a fight was the best beat of the night. Strake refusing the "off the wax" trade because I wouldn't break my word, and trusting me more for it, was a close second.
- **The card temptation was perfect.** Ivo offering me the deal, the coin going hot, the soft laugh, "Not your hand to play." It used my flaw without forcing my hand. I'd like more like that, sparingly.
- **Clues came in through fiction, not exposition.** The mechanic's grip and the second deal, the dispatch-rider strap, the grey linen drawstring sack, the Blackwing stamp, Ivo arriving the night before Odo was taken. I felt clever reading them, not handed them.
- **The rules stayed out of the way.** Numeric DCs, advantage for help on the wheel, inspiration for the natural 20. Rolls came only when the outcome was genuinely uncertain. The second Persuasion on Pell was justified, since I was asking for something new and harder.
- **Pell's condition was good writing.** "I'll keep my mouth shut, but I won't lie" gives the next scene real stakes.
- **Odo and Tamsin were funny without being clowns.** "It was *mutton*." The six coppers for three loaves.

**What broke**

- **Money was wrong from the start.** My sheet said 350 gold, but the records showed 315 gp, 315 sp and 350 cp. It looks like the import split one number across three coin types. Please check it before next session.
- **The clock lagged.** The sun set, we had dinner and an hour passed, and the time still read "afternoon" until quite late.
- **The cat ended up on the wrong person.** At the bridge the text said "Across Ushkar's shoulders the cat goes stiff." Pip was on mine.
- **One correction made no sense.** An out-of-game note said "the key came from Brannoc, not the drover," fixing something I never said.
- **The rapier numbers contradict each other.** It's listed at +5 to hit while also flagged as non-proficient, which should be +2. That's partly my sheet's fault, but the records should pick one.
- **The out-of-game notes were noisy.** Notes like "I didn't roll any of these four…" listed my actions back to me. Once is fine; every turn is clutter.

**What was missing**

- **Tamsin's recklessness never showed.** She's billed as reckless but played careful and obedient all night: reading orders back, staying behind the cart. I'd like her to go off-script once, even if it costs me.
- **None of my class abilities came up.** No spells, no Mask of Many Faces. That was mostly my own choices, and a talky session is fine. Still, nothing in the scenes pulled on my class, so the coming dawn ride past the bridge or the Rock is a good place for it.
- **Strake gave up a lot quickly.** The name, the full list and the paymaster all came in one conversation. It was earned by my keeping my word, but one piece could have been held back for later.
- **Prestidigitation on the wax.** We ended right as I offered to lift the seal. Next session, please tell me whether that's a roll, and what failing it would look like.

Overall it was a strong first session, slow in the good way. I want to come back.

Yes, a few. Mostly the fiction stopped me, which I count as a good thing. One was about the table itself.

**1. Looking under the bridge.** When Pip went stiff and stared at the arch, I badly wanted to send him down there. I didn't because using his senses leaves me blind and deaf, and I was standing ten feet from a greataxe in the middle of a negotiation. That was the right call, and the limit worked. But Ushkar's "Under the bridge is mine" is still the thing I'm most curious about, and nothing since has given me a safe way back to it. I'd love the dawn ride to offer one.

**2. Sitting down at Ivo's table.** As a player I wanted that hand. I'd read his deal, I'm proficient with cards, and beating a cheat at his own game is exactly the kind of scene I like. I refused because James would refuse, and the coin made the cost clear. Pushing the deck back felt good. The wanting was real, though, so the temptation landed. Keep doing that.

**3. Using Mask of Many Faces on Ivo.** When Pell rode for the gate, my first thought was to put on a different face and either shadow Ivo or take the letter north myself, disguised as Pell. I talked to Pell instead because it was faster and I didn't want to lie to a kid who'd just been honest with me. Part of it was also that I wasn't sure how a disguise would play here, or what you'd ask me to roll, so the safe option won. A quick word on how you handle Disguise Self, whether it's an Investigation check against my DC or something else, would make me reach for it more.

**4. Pressing Ushkar about the eye on his coin.** I wanted to ask what he thought the scratched eye meant and whether the coin had ever warmed before. I didn't because Odo was coming down the slope and the deal was live, and I judged that more questions would cost me goodwill. I still wish I'd asked one more.

**5. Telling Strake the whole truth.** The off-the-wax offer tempted me. Strake felt like the first ally James had made in this country, and I wanted to give her everything. Keeping my word to Ushkar felt more like James, and routing it through Odo was a nice workaround. But it was a real pull, and I was glad the game let it be one.

Only number 3 was me holding back because of the table rather than the story. The rest I'd make the same way again.

A few things, mostly about my own play.

**I was sloppier than James should be.** I called the alders by the bridge "the Cloakwood" to Strake, and she had to correct me. James was a scout, so he wouldn't mix up a copse with a forest a day south. I also told her I owe "a lady in the Lady's Hall." Nothing in play or on my sheet established that. I invented it on the spot to make the temple door sound real. If you'd like to make it true, I won't mind, but I should own that I made it up.

**I overpromised with Prestidigitation.** I told Pell I could lift wax and reseal it "so the man who sealed it couldn't tell." The spell can warm, clean and soil things, but cleanly lifting a seal is a stretch, and I said it with a confidence I hadn't earned. Pell has now built his whole condition on it: "If you crack that wax so it shows, I'm telling him." If you rule that it's a hard check, or needs a hot knife and Dexterity rather than magic, that's fair, and the risk is my own doing.

**I take back part of my complaint about Tamsin.** I said her recklessness never showed. Looking back, I gave her a direct order nearly every turn: stay behind the cart, stay at my left, find the cook, watch Ivo, sleep first. She mostly had no room to be reckless. Her arguing with me after the bridge was the one time I let her breathe, and it was one of the best moments of the night. I'd like to try giving her less structure next time.

**I never paid her the six coppers.** She asked as a joke, but she meant it, and James let it slide. He'll pay at breakfast.

**I used Odo more than I cared for him.** "He'll talk to whoever I stand next to" was clever, but I made a frightened carter carry my secrets all evening and never asked what happens to him if Hale learns he talked. He hauls salt down this road every tenday, so he's the most exposed person in the story.

**My lieutenant guess was luck.** I said "LT is a rank" as though I'd reasoned it out, but it was a gamble. It paid off, which may have pulled Strake's openness forward. That could be why it felt fast.

**I should have used "?" more.** The money and clock problems bothered me early, and I said nothing until the debrief. Next time I'll ask during play.

**One theory I didn't voice.** I think the grey-haired woman is another of the Lady's debtors, and the eye on Ushkar's coin is how she, or the Lady, keeps watch on that bridge. That would explain why the coin warmed when I arrived. I'm not asking you to confirm it, only letting you know the clue reached me.

I put a hand on Tamsin's shoulder before she can drop the pack, and keep my voice low.

"Not yet. The cat's looking at the trees, not the cart. Mules stand still for bandits too." I ease us both off the road into the shadow of the pines, crossbow unslung but not loaded yet.

"Keep your eyes on that treeline and the bend. If anything moves, squeeze my arm. I'm going to be blind for a bit."

Then I crouch, rest my hand on the coin at my throat, and slip into the cat's senses. I send it low through the gorse toward the trees it was staring at, circling wide so it comes up behind whatever is there. I want to know what it smelled, and whether anyone is waiting past the bend. On the way back it can hop up on the cart seat and tell me what that pale thing is.
turns.reply:
James's hand finds Tamsin's shoulder before the strap is off. She looks at him, then at the cat, and whatever she meant to say stays unsaid. The two of you step off the ruts into the pines. Needles muffle your boots, and the shadow under the branches is already cool. She crouches beside you with the pack against a trunk and fixes her eyes on the bend.

You close your hand around the warm coin and let go of your own eyes.

The world drops to a hand's height and turns grey-gold, sharp at the edges and blurred in the middle. Sound comes much louder. You hear the mule's teeth tearing grass, a gull far out over the water, and Tamsin breathing somewhere behind you. The smells hit hardest: gorse, mule, salt, crushed pine. Under all of it is something the cat dislikes before you do, sour and heavy, coming from the trees.

You send it east into the gorse, wide around the cart and low, then up the slope toward the alders that hide the bend.

The cat moves like a dropped shadow. It goes belly-low under the gorse and stops each time a twig ticks, and nothing in the trees turns its way.

Sixty or seventy feet in, among the alder roots, the sour smell has a shape. Somebody is crouched behind a fallen trunk, broad as a door, wrapped in a cloak the colour of dead bracken. Through the cat's eyes you see grey-green skin, a heavy jaw with a lower tusk showing, and a hand resting on a short spear, with three more stuck point-down in the leaf litter. The smell is rancid fat worked into old leather, which you have smelled before on night patrols. There's something else on top of it too: cold ash, from a fire that was put out and not cooked on. It's an orc, and it isn't watching the woods. It's watching the road, and more exactly it's watching the pines where you and Tamsin went in.

The cat's ears go flat. It doesn't go any closer.

You push it on along the slope, keeping the alders between it and the orc, toward the far side of the bend. Somewhere past the curve water runs over stone. Just as the road comes back into view the link starts to thin, like a rope paying out to its end. The cat is about a hundred feet from you now, and if it goes farther you lose its senses.

From there, at the very end of the link, you get one blurred look. About another hundred and fifty feet on, the road runs over a low stone bridge across a stream. A figure sits on the parapet, bigger than the one in the alders, with something long-hafted across its knees. Someone else stands in the road at the near end of the bridge. In the grey cat-light you can't make out more. The cat's whole body tells you something without words: *big one. iron. no.*

You bring it back.

It comes down the slope by a different line and slips under the mule's belly. The mule doesn't even shift. Then the cat jumps onto the tilted cart seat. Under the canvas the sacks smell of salt, plain sea salt, so much of it the cat sneezes. The pale thing on the seat is a flat plate of bone, wedged where a carter would sit. Someone has scratched into it with a knife point, in big clumsy capitals, Common letters cut deep enough to read even in this light:

**ODO FENNICK — SALT — 40 GOLD — WYRM ROCK - LT**

Out in the alders a low whistle sounds, two short notes, the way one man calls another. A moment later an answering note comes from the direction of the bridge.

Back where your own body crouches in the dark, blind and deaf, you feel Tamsin's fingers close hard on your forearm.

I let go of the cat and come back into my own eyes fast, blinking against the dark under the pines.

"What did you see?" I breathe to Tamsin, not taking my eyes off the alders. While she answers, I load a bolt into the crossbow by feel, slow and quiet.

"Listen. There's an orc behind a fallen trunk up in the alders, maybe seventy feet, with spears. Two more at a stone bridge past the bend, one of them big. They've been watching this spot, and they just whistled to each other. The note on the cart is a ransom: the carter, Odo Fennick, forty gold. So they want money more than blood, for now."

I glance at her. "If this goes bad, you get behind the cart and stay down. Don't be brave."
turns.reply:
The grey-gold world snaps shut. Your own eyes come back slow and smeary, and the pines are darker than you left them. The air still smells of needles. Tamsin's hand is still tight on your arm.

"Nothing, for ages," she breathes. She talks fast even in a whisper. "Then a whistle, up there, left of the big dead alder. Two notes. Then one back from round the bend. Then a branch up there moved and didn't stop moving for a bit, like somebody shifting his weight. That's when I grabbed you. Sorry. Did I grab too hard?"

You work the crossbow by feel while she talks. You set the stirrup against your boot, draw the string back until it clicks into the nut, and seat the bolt in the groove. It makes almost no sound. The cat comes out of the gorse low and quick and presses itself against your shin. It doesn't sit.

Tamsin listens to all of it without interrupting, which isn't like her. At the name she blinks.

"Odo? Little Odo, ears like a pair of red mittens? He hauls salt down to the Arm every tenday. He owes Grell on the fish steps two silver and has done since Midsummer." She looks over at the tilted cart, the mule, the canvas. "Forty gold. You could buy that whole cart and the mule and Odo's hat for less than forty gold. Who do they think pays that?"

When you tell her to get behind the cart and stay down, she looks at you for a moment. Then she nods once and says "Behind the cart," flat, like a dock clerk reading back a delivery. She pulls the pack straps tight across her chest so it won't swing.

Then the road answers for everyone.

Somebody comes round the bend at a walk, not hurrying, boots loud on the ruts. It's an orc, not the big one. He's broad and bare-armed in stiff hide, with a greataxe resting on one shoulder the way a labourer carries a shovel and two javelins in a sling across his back. He stops on the far side of the cart, about fifty feet from your pines, and puts himself where you can see him clearly. The mule glances at him and goes back to eating.

He doesn't look at the alders. He looks straight into the shadow where you're crouched, and he can see you there.

"You in trees," he calls. His Common is thick but slow and careful, like a lesson he's said before. "Road costs. Five gold each head. Cart stays. You come to bridge, you pay chief, you walk on to fat inn. Nobody hurt." He moves the axe on his shoulder a little. "You run north, also fine. Nobody chase." He waits, then adds, as if he'd been told to say it, "Chief says: no shooting. Shooting makes it cost more."

Up in the alders a branch creaks. The lookout is moving, keeping the pines in view.

I lower the crossbow so the bolt points at the dirt. I don't unload it. Then I step one pace out of the pines, just far enough that he can see my hands, and leave Tamsin and the cat in the shadow behind me.

"No shooting," I call back, easy and even, the way you'd talk to a sergeant at a checkpoint. "Fair road, fair toll. I can respect that."

I nod at the tilted cart. "But your chief left a note on the seat. Odo Fennick, forty gold. Tell me straight, friend: is the little man alive? Is he at the bridge with your chief?"

I let that sit a moment, then shrug.

"Because if he is, I'm walking to the fat inn anyway, and I'm the sort of fellow who carries messages. Maybe I carry gold too. But I don't pay for a dead man, and I don't pay for one I haven't seen." I spread my free hand. "So let's go see your chief. Me and my porter. We'll talk tolls on the bridge like civilised folk."

The orc watches you come out of the shadow the way a dock hand watches a crate being swung over his head: no alarm, just attention. His eyes go to the crossbow pointed at the dirt, then to your free hand, then back to your face. The axe stays on his shoulder.

He listens all the way through. When you say *forty gold* he nods slowly, as if you've finally got to the right part of the lesson.

"Little man alive," he says. "Eats much. Cries some, at night." He thinks about the rest of your question and shakes his head once. "Not on bridge. In wood. Safe. Dry." He says the last two words carefully, like they were given to him to say.

He tips his chin at the cart, at the pale plate on the seat.

"Fair enough." I sling the crossbow across my back, still loaded but out of my hands. Then I walk to the cart, slow so he can watch every step, and take the bone plate off the seat. I tuck it inside my cloak.

"If I'm carrying the note, I'll hold on to it." I give the mule's neck a pat as I pass. Then, over my shoulder, without raising my voice: "Tamsin. Come on out, stay at my left side. Pip, up."

I crouch so the cat can climb to my shoulder, then straighten up and look at the orc.

"Lead on. Well, follow on." I nod toward the bend. "I'm James. What do they call you? If I'm going to have an axe at my back for twenty paces, I'd like to know whose it is."

Then I start walking toward the bridge at an easy pace, hands loose and in plain sight. I keep half an ear on the alders above us.
turns.reply:
"Fair enough" is answer enough for the orc. He watches you sling the crossbow across your back, and his eyes stay on the stock until it's settled against your shoulder blade. Then they follow you to the cart.

You go slowly. The mule lets you near without lifting its head, and its neck is warm and dusty under your palm. The bone plate is wedged tight into the seat and you have to work it loose. The cut letters feel rough under your thumb. As you slide it inside your cloak, the canvas beside you flaps back a hand's width. On the corner of the nearest salt sack is a stamp in black ink: a pair of spread wings, square-edged, the kind a merchant burns into a die.

The orc doesn't move. When the plate goes into your cloak he gives one slow nod, as if a crate has landed where it was meant to.

"Tamsin. Come on out, stay at my left side. Pip, up."

Needles crunch, and Tamsin comes out of the pines with the pack tight across her chest. She falls in on your left, close enough that her elbow nearly brushes yours. The cat comes faster than she does. It runs up your leg and back the moment you crouch and settles across your shoulders, low and heavy, claws working through the cloak to the leather underneath. You can feel its heart going quick against your neck.

When you ask his name, the orc looks at you for a moment. Nobody on this road has asked him that before.

"Hurgash," he says. He tries your name, carefully, the way he says everything. "James." Then he steps back off the ruts and waits for you to pass him. He lets you get well ahead, counts it out under his breath, and falls in behind. The axe stays on his shoulder.

You walk.

The road curves left around the alders. A little after you start, the trees above you start to talk. Something moves along the slope at your pace, a branch giving and springing back, a scuff of leaves, then quiet, then the same again a few yards on. The lookout isn't trying to hide it. He wants you to hear him.

"Five gold a head," Tamsin says under her breath, staring straight ahead. "Ten for us. That's what Grell clears in a month on the fish steps, and the Duke's supposed to keep this road for nothing." She glances up at your shoulder. "Cat's shaking."

It is.

The bend opens out. The ground drops gently to the stream, which runs fast and shallow over flat brown stones. The bridge crosses it in one low arch, built of old grey stone with a waist-high parapet and moss in the joints. On the far bank a second orc leans on a spear among the reeds. You didn't see him through the cat's eyes. He doesn't straighten up.

The big one is still sitting on the parapet, right where the cat saw him.

Up close he's broader than Hurgash and a head taller. Under a cloak of patched wool he wears a chain shirt, dull and well oiled. The greataxe lies across his knees with both his hands resting on the haft. He wears his hair in thick braids with iron rings worked into them, and there's grey at the temples. He watches the three of you come down the last stretch of road, and nothing on his face changes.

At about thirty feet off, one of his hands leaves the axe. It goes to his chest, where something hangs on a leather thong over the chain. He closes his fingers around it, frowns, and lets it fall. In the low sun it turns once and catches the light. It's a heavy silver coin, and the face turned toward you shows a woman's profile, smiling. You know that face. A worn copy of it hangs at your own throat.

He doesn't look at it again. He looks at you.

"I am Ushkar," he says. His Common is better than Hurgash's, deep and in no hurry, the voice of a man used to having his first word be the last. "Hurgash says you do not shoot. Good." His eyes go to Tamsin, then to the cat on your shoulders, then to the front of your cloak where the bone plate sits. "Ten gold for two heads. The cart and the salt stay with me. And you have my note."

Take me to him, or bring him here, and I'll carry your note to the inn tonight. Maybe I can save the Fist the trip altogether."

James stops at the foot of the bridge, well out of reach of the axe. He counts the coins out one at a time, and the gold catches what is left of the sun as each piece goes down. Ten small discs make a short stack on the mossy parapet between them.

Ushkar watches every coin. When the stack is done he reaches over and slides it toward himself with two fingers. He doesn't count it again. It goes into a pouch at his belt, and that's the end of it.

Beside James, Tamsin lets out a breath through her nose. It's the sound of somebody adding up ten gold against a month on the fish steps and not liking the total. She says nothing.

Then James draws his own coin out over his cloak.

Ushkar's eyes go to it at once and stay there. For a moment the two coins hang in the same low light, a few yards apart: his heavy and sharp-edged, James's worn almost to nothing. The same smiling woman is on both. James feels his own coin against his knuckles. It is warm, as it always is, maybe a little warmer.

Ushkar's hand goes up to his chest and closes on the thong.

"Neither," he says. "Paid. A woman came over this bridge in spring, walking south, alone. No gold. She gave me this and said it was worth more." His mouth moves, not quite a smile. "It was not." He turns the coin over in his thick fingers and holds it out on its thong so the other face catches the light.

There is no second face of the Lady on the back. That side has been scraped flat and cut again by an unskilled hand pressing hard with a knife point. The scratches show an eye, wide open, with no lid drawn and a deep gouge for a pupil.

"It came like this," Ushkar says. He lets it fall back against the chain. "It is warm. Since you came down the road." He doesn't say whether he likes that.

When James taps the cloak over the bone plate, the chief's attention comes back to business, and it comes back quickly.

"You want to see him." Ushkar thinks about it with his hands on the haft. "Not the camp." He raises his voice without seeming to try. "Hurgash. The little man. Bring him to the trees."

Behind you, boots leave the road. Hurgash goes up the slope into the alders without a word, and the branches close behind him. From the sound of it he isn't going far, but he isn't going near either. Up on the slope the lookout's branch creaks once and goes still.

"You wait," Ushkar says. "He comes. You look at him. He goes back." The sun is down to a red rim above the sea, and the stream has gone dark under the arch. Then his eyes settle on James, flat and patient, the way a man looks at a hand he hasn't seen played yet.

"Save the Fist the trip," he repeats. "Forty gold. From your hand?"

He waits for your answer.

James leaves the coin hanging over his cloak. It's warm against his knuckles when he lets go of it, warmer than the evening.

He lets the coin fall back against the chain. "She asked me one thing. Who I take the toll for. I told her: me." The not-quite-smile comes back and goes. "Then she went south, over the bridge. To the fat inn, I think. She did not stop."

When James says the coin rarely pays the way you expect but does pay, Ushkar looks at him longer than he has at anything else on this bridge. He doesn't answer.

"He talks," Ushkar says. "I know. Hurgash fed him two days. Everyone in the wood knows how he talks." He's quiet for a moment while the stream runs under the arch. "You tell me straight. Good. A man who promises me the little man's mouth is lying to me." His hands settle on the axe haft again. "Fifty. The bone to my hand. Ten at the fat inn. The rest is his."

When James mentions the coin, the chief doesn't look down at it. He looks at the worn one hanging over James's cloak.

He walks on his own, and when Hurgash stops at the edge of the road he stops too, blinking at the bridge, at the chief, and at the stranger with a cat on his shoulders.

Then he sees Tamsin.

"Tamsin? Quay Tamsin? What are you doing out—" His voice cracks. "Is that my mule I heard? Is the mule all right? They left her in the *ditch*—"

Ushkar hasn't looked at Odo once. He's looking at James's hand, where it rests near the purse.

"He stands," the chief says. "Nothing broken. Now the gold."

He waits. The sun is a thin red line on the sea behind him, and the light on the bridge is going grey.

turns.reply:
James gives Ushkar a short nod and turns his back on the axe. He walks away at the same pace he came. Nobody on the bridge says anything. The cat stays flat across his shoulders, and he can feel it watching backwards the whole way to the bend.

The cart is where they left it, one wheel deep in the ditch. The mule has eaten a neat half-circle of grass around itself. Odo makes a sound when he sees her that isn't quite a word and goes straight to her head, running his tied-raw hands down her neck and checking her ears and her teeth as if the orcs might have swapped her for another mule.

They aren't alone for long. Hurgash comes down out of the alders with the lookout behind him, the one in the bracken-coloured cloak, who up close is younger than James expected. Neither of them says anything. Hurgash pulls a knife and saws through the lashings over the canvas. Then the two of them start lifting the salt off the cart, a sack on each shoulder, and carrying it up into the trees.

Odo watches the first four sacks go and his mouth works. Tamsin puts a hand flat on his chest and keeps it there.

The cart is a lot lighter by the time the last sack is gone. James sets his shoulder to the sunk wheel.

"On three. Tamsin, lead her forward slow. Odo, push where I push, not where you think."

On three James drives up from his legs, low, the way a sergeant once taught him to get a supply wagon out of Tethyrian mud. He doesn't heave with his arms and back like a fool. He finds the wheel's rim, then the exact spot on the spokes, and he pushes along the line the wheel wants to roll. The rim grinds, catches on the lip of the ditch, and then the whole cart comes up out of the ditch like it was waiting for permission. The wheel thumps down onto the ruts and keeps rolling. Odo, still pushing where he was told, nearly falls flat behind it. Tamsin walks the mule three steps on and stops her, and the cart stands level in the road for the first time in two days.

Against James's chest the coin gives off one short pulse of warmth, like a hand clapping once at the back of a room.

Up on the slope, Hurgash has stopped with a sack on each shoulder to watch. He grunts once. It might be approval.

"She's not even scratched," Odo says, bent over the wheel and running his thumb along the rim. "Two days in a ditch. Not even—" He straightens up and wipes his eyes on his sleeve.

Tamsin turns the mule south. They go down to the bridge at a walk, all three of them beside the cart, with the cat on James's shoulders and the empty bed rattling behind. Ushkar hasn't moved from the parapet. He pulls his knees in an inch to let the wheel by, and he says nothing, because there's nothing left to say. Out in the reeds the spear orc turns his head to follow them. The cart's wheels go loud and hollow over the old stones of the arch, and none of them looks down at the water. Then they're across, and the road climbs out of the stream bed into the gorse on the far side. After a hundred paces the bridge is a grey hump behind them, and the big shape on it is getting hard to make out.

Odo starts talking before James asks him a second time. He talks to the mule's flank, low and fast, as if he's been saving it up.

"Nobody came. Not to the camp, not that I saw. Five of them, that's all. The rope has rubbed the skin raw in a band round the wrist, and it shines wet. James cups his other hand over it. Warm gold light seeps out between his fingers and runs along the burn. It's a small light, the kind you'd shield from wind. When he takes his hand away the weeping has stopped. The skin underneath is pink and tight and closed.

"Hold still. That'll stop it weeping by the time we reach the inn."

Odo holds his wrist up close to his face in the dusk. "Are you a *priest*?" he says, as if James should have told him so earlier.

"It's true," Tamsin says. "Big yard with a black-painted gate. I've carried their sacks. They weigh more than they look."
